name: Cartridge razor

lead: A cartridge razor clips a disposable multi-blade head onto a handle. It has been the dominant style of razor since the 1970s, and the payoff is a close, clean shave visible right after.

Several blades set in a row cut the hair in successive passes, and the cartridge snaps off when dull. Wilkinson introduced the design in 1970 and Gillette followed in 1971; makers have steadily added blades since. In one 2024 study of 59 men, a three-blade cartridge left more shaving-induced redness than a safety razor.

paras: People use it with shaving cream or gel and replace the cartridge when it dulls. Cartridges are proprietary, so buyers stay with their handle's brand, and results last until the hair regrows.
Razor-related redness and irritation were higher with a three-blade cartridge than a safety razor in the 2024 study. Cuts are possible with any razor.

angle.text: The cartridge razor is the standard tool for a close, clean shave, with a smooth groomed face visible right after. In one study of 59 men it left more redness than a safety razor.

lead: A cartridge razor is a manual razor whose blades, typically two to six or more, are mounted in a disposable plastic cartridge that clips onto a reusable handle. Cartridge and disposable razors have been the predominant type of razor since the 1970s.[1]

The design was introduced commercially in 1970 by Wilkinson, whose Bonded Shaving System embedded a single blade in a disposable cartridge, and Gillette answered in 1971 with the twin-blade Trac II.[1] Manufacturers have since added blades, and market commentary and Wikipedia note that multi-blade cartridges carry high profit margins and tie buyers to proprietary cartridges.[1]

One 2024 study in 59 men compared a cartridge razor with a safety razor and found more shaving-induced redness with the cartridge.[2] Beyond this, little controlled research on cartridge razors appears.

paras: Wilkinson's 1970 system placed one blade in a disposable cartridge. Gillette's 1971 Trac II used two blades, and Gillette claimed the pair gave a closer shave through a hysteresis effect, a claim whose practical importance Wikipedia says has been questioned.[1] Bic launched the fully disposable razor in 1974, and Gillette's Good News followed in the US in 1976.[1]

The three-blade Mach3 appeared in 1998, after which Gillette's blade sales are reported to have risen 50 percent; Schick responded with the four-blade Quattro. A five-blade Gillette razor reached the market in 2006, and Dorco released six- and later seven-blade cartridges starting in 2012.[1] Gillette's vibrating Fusion Power and M3Power models were the subject of a US court ruling that their vibration claims were unsubstantiated and inaccurate.[1]

A 2024 study used multispectral near-infrared spectroscopy imaging to measure shaving-induced erythema in 59 healthy men, shaving one side of the face or neck with a safety razor and the other with a three-blade cartridge razor.[2] Skin oxygen saturation measurements showed significantly less erythema with the safety razor: immediately after shaving, 40.3 percent of safety-razor skin was affected versus 57.6 percent for the cartridge razor, and 36.5 versus 53.8 percent at five minutes.[2] The study compared a single safety-razor and a single cartridge design, so its findings apply to those products.
Shaving-induced redness is a recognised inflammatory skin response, and the 2024 study identifies it as a quantifiable outcome of razor choice.[2] Cuts and irritation can occur with any razor.
